short.text: Deula is the local word for a temple. Used alone, it often means just the main shrine with its tower.

sources.locator: scan leaves 212 and 385, glossary (printed pages unverified)

short.note: Debala Mitra's ASI guide: 'general name for a temple as a whole; when used singly, it refers to the sanctuary'. Percy Brown (1959) says the same. Spellings vary: deul (Mitra, Brown), deula (Behera).

long.text: Odisha's temples come in three main types: rekha, pidha and khakhara.
long.note: Debala Mitra sorts Bhubaneswar's temples into 'Rekha, Pidha and Khakhara orders'. K.S. Behera says the local silpa texts 'mention three types of structures'. N.K. Bose (1932) counts four types in Orissa, adding the rare Gauriya, and calls the pidha type 'Bhadra'.

long.text: A typical Odisha temple joins two types. A rekha tower rises over the shrine, and a pidha hall stands in front of it.

sources.locator: Vol. I, scan leaf 227 (printed page unverified)

long.note: Percy Brown: the deul and the jagamohan 'combined constitute the essentials of the Orissan temple type'. Mitra's example is Konark.

long.text: From bottom to top, a temple has four parts: the pista (platform), bada (wall), gandi (tower or roof) and mastaka (crown).
long.note: N.K. Bose (1932) names the four parts and says 'mastaka' is a name coined for convenience. K.S. Behera also calls the crown 'shira'. Percy Brown (1959) uses other names for the tower's parts. The platform is spelled pista (Bose, Brown), pishta (Mitra) or pitha (Behera).

long.text: Many part names come from the human body, such as foot, leg, trunk, throat and head. Scholars say the temple was pictured as a body.
long.note: N.K. Bose (1932): 'the Rekha temple has been likened to the human body'. Debala Mitra: naming parts after human limbs 'suggests that temples were likened to the human body'. K.S. Behera goes further: the craftsmen 'considered the temple as the body of the Cosmic Being'.

short.text: A rekha deula has a tall, curved tower. The tower rises almost straight at first, then curves inward more and more near the top.
short.note: N.K. Bose (1932) compares the outline to 'a tall bamboo-post which has been slightly bent towards the top by a rope'. Mitra's ASI glossary: 'a curvilinear tower which presents the appearance of a continuous line'.

long.text: The rekha form is usually used for the main shrine, the sanctuary.

sources.locator: Vol. I, scan leaf 227 (printed page unverified)

long.note: K.S. Behera: 'usually limited to the main temple'. Stella Kramrisch calls the sanctuary the 'Rekha or Bara Deul'. Mitra's example is Konark, whose rekha tower has fallen.

short.text: A pidha deula has a roof like a stepped pyramid. It is built from flat layers, called pidhas, that get smaller as they rise.
short.note: N.K. Bose (1932) calls this type 'Bhadra'. K.S. Behera: the uppermost pidha is generally 'half the size of the lowest one'.

long.text: The pidha form is mostly used for a temple's halls: the jagamohana, the dance hall and the hall of offerings.
long.note: Mitra's ASI glossary: 'usually limited to the jagamohana, bhoga-mandapa and nata-mandapa in Orissa'.

long.text: The stepped pidha roof came later. In the earliest temples, the hall in front had a lower, flatter roof.
long.note: K.S. Behera: in the earlier phase the jagamohana 'was distinguished by a flat roof'. K.C. Panigrahi: the early porch is 'a low mandapa', and the pidha form first appears as the porch of the Mukteshvara.

long.text: The pidha hall in front of the shrine is also called a bhadra deula, or a mukhasala, which means 'front hall'.
long.note: Bose (1932): the Bhadra is also called the Mukhasala, 'the building which is placed towards the face or front of the Rekha'. Mitra glosses bhadra deul as 'auspicious temple'.

short.text: A khakhara deula has an oblong (rectangular) plan. Its roof is long and rounded on top, like half a barrel lying on its side.
short.note: N.K. Bose (1932): the ground plan of the khakhara 'is rectangular'. K.S. Behera: 'oblong bada and semi-cylindrical roof'. Mitra's ASI guide calls the roofs of its carved models 'wagon-vaulted'.

long.text: Two khakhara temples in Bhubaneswar are the Vaital Deul and the small Gauri temple.
The name khakhara comes from the kakharu, a kind of pumpkin-gourd. The temple's long, rounded roof looks a little like it.
long.note: Debala Mitra (1960): the name is 'due to the faint resemblance of the barrel-vaulted elongated roof of its temples with a variety of pumpkin-gourd, called kakharu in Oriya'. She links the local name vaitalu for this gourd with the name of the Vaital Deul.

long.text: This roof shape may copy very old halls, whose rounded roofs rested on timber or bent bamboo.
long.note: Debala Mitra (1960): the roof 'is a modified survival of the primitive halls with a semi-cylindrical roof resting on a framework of timber or bent split bamboos (in the case of a thatched roof)'.

long.text: Khakhara temples are often linked with the worship of goddesses. But goddesses are also found in temples of other types, and experts do not all agree about the Vaital Deul.
long.note: K.S. Behera (2005): the khakhara temple is 'used for Devi worship'. Debala Mitra (1960): the available evidence 'indicates that temples of this Order in Orissa belonged to the Sakta cult, though the converse is not true', as goddesses also sit in rekha temples such as the Mohini and Chitrakarini. Percy Brown (1959) calls the Vaital Deul 'a Siva temple of the Orissan group'.

long.text: Full khakhara temples are rare.
long.note: N.K. Bose (1932): the type 'is limited to six examples in Bhubaneswar', but its miniatures are very common as decoration.

short.text: A khakhara-mundi is a small carved model of a khakhara temple. Many temple walls are decorated with them.
short.note: Mitra's ASI glossary: 'miniature representation of a khakhara temple as an ornamental motif'. Bose (1932): such miniatures 'were very extensively employed as a decorative motif'. Konark's walls have many (Mitra, scan leaves 46 and 53).

short.text: The main shrine is also called the bada deula, which means 'big temple'. This bada means 'big'. It is a different word from bada, the wall.

sources.locator: Vol. I, scan leaf 227 (printed page unverified)

short.note: Mitra's ASI glossary: 'bada deul literally big temple, meaning the sanctuary'; the same glossary lists 'bada ... wall' as a separate entry. Kramrisch writes 'Bara Deul'.

short.text: The main shrine with its tower is also called the vimana.
short.note: K.S. Behera: 'The main temple or the Vimana (also called deula)'. Percy Brown: deul can mean 'the sanctuary only, such as the cella and its tower, the vimana'.

short.text: The silpa sastras are Odisha's traditional building manuals. Temple builders followed them.
short.note: K.S. Behera: 'In the construction of temples, Silpasastra texts are followed.' Debala Mitra calls them 'Orissan Silpa-sastras or architectural canons'.

long.text: The names rekha, pidha and khakhara are found in these manuals. There, the pidha type is also called bhadra.
long.note: N.K. Bose (1932): 'in the silpasastras, there are specifications of 55 Rekha, 6 Bhadra and 3 Khakhara temples'. K.C. Panigrahi: 'In the canons of Orissan architecture it is known as the Pidha or Bhadra type'. K.S. Behera: the local texts 'mention three types of structures, rekha, pidha and khakara'.

short.text: The jagamohana is the hall in front of the main shrine, where worshippers gather. It usually has a pidha (stepped) roof.

sources.locator: scan leaves 25 and 100, glossary (printed pages unverified)

short.note: Mitra's ASI glossary: 'hall in front of a sanctuary, usually in a pidha temple'. The earliest halls did not have a stepped roof yet.

long.text: The word jagamohana is explained as 'that which pleases the whole world'.
long.note: N.K. Bose's glossary (1932): 'Jagamohan — That which pleases the whole world; that which is most pleasing'.

short.text: The natamandira is the dance hall. In large temples it stands in front of the jagamohana.
short.note: Names vary: Nat Mandir (Brown), nata mandapa (Mitra), Nata-mandira (Behera). Mitra's glossary calls it a 'festive hall'; her Lingaraja text, Brown and Behera say 'dancing hall'.

long.text: In the largest temples, four buildings stand in one straight line: deula, jagamohana, natamandira and bhogamandapa. The two front halls were often added later. The Lingaraja Temple and the Jagannath Temple in Puri both have all four.
long.note: Debala Mitra: the Lingaraja 'consists of the customary four structures', 'disposed on the same axis but do not necessarily belong to the same period'; at Puri the nata and bhoga-mandapas are 'later additions'. Percy Brown: the extra halls 'were added to the front of the assembly hall'.

short.text: The bhogamandapa is the hall of offering. It usually stands in front of the dance hall.
short.note: Percy Brown and K.S. Behera also call it 'the refectory hall of a temple', a dining hall. At Konark the detached hall in front is named both ways: Mitra says it 'is generally believed to be a nata-mandapa' and 'is also known as the bhoga-mandapa'.

short.text: The pista is the platform or base that a temple stands on. Not every temple has one.

sources.locator: scan leaves 88 and 101, glossary (printed pages unverified)
scan leaves 107 and 291, glossary (printed pages unverified)

short.note: N.K. Bose (1932): the pista 'does not form an essential part of the temple proper'; the Lingaraja has none. Spellings: pista (Bose, Brown), pishta (Mitra), pitha (Behera).

short.text: The bada is the upright wall of the temple. It stands between the platform and the tower or roof.
short.note: N.K. Bose spells it 'bara'. It is not the same word as the 'bada' in bada deula, which means 'big'.

long.text: Early temples mostly have the three-part wall. The five-part wall is found in later temples.
long.note: N.K. Bose (1932) found that the Bhubaneswar temples he could date early 'have a bara composed of three elements', and that five parts appear 'only in the later temples'. Debala Mitra's ASI guide, describing Konark, says the wall has five divisions 'as in all Orissa temples'; that describes the fully developed temples. The dating rests on style.

short.text: The gandi is the main body of the tower or roof, above the wall. The word means 'trunk', as in the trunk of a body.
short.note: Mitra's ASI glossary: 'literally trunk; curvilinear spire or pyramidal roof above bada and below the mastaka'. Percy Brown (1959) calls the tall middle part of the tower the 'chhapra' instead.

short.text: The mastaka is the crown: the stack of round parts on top of the tower. The word means 'head'.

sources.locator: scan leaves 26 and 101, glossary (printed pages unverified)

short.note: Mitra's ASI glossary: 'head; crowning elements above the gandi'. Bose (1932): its elements 'are all circular in cross-section'.

long.text: The name mastaka is modern. It was made up to make the crown easier to talk about.

sources.locator: scan leaves 134 and 289, glossary (printed pages unverified)

long.note: N.K. Bose (1932): 'The mastaka (a name which has been coined for the sake of convenience)'. Debala Mitra and K.S. Behera use it as the standard term; Behera also gives 'shira'.

short.text: The pabhaga is the 'foot' of the wall. It is a stack of three to five shaped stone bands, called mouldings, at the very bottom.
short.note: N.K. Bose (1932): 'Division corresponding to the foot; set of three, four or five mouldings at the base of a temple'.

long.text: Often the foot has five mouldings, named khura, kumbha, pata, kani and basanta. Some temples have only three or four.
long.note: K.S. Behera: the pabhaga 'is composed of mouldings called khura, kumbha, pata, kani and basanta'. One passage in Bose (1932) puts 'kalasa' in place of kumbha; his glossary says kalasa can '(rarely)' mean the kumbha moulding.

short.text: The kumbha is one of the mouldings in the foot of the wall. It is shaped like a water-pot, and kumbha means 'water-pot'.

sources.locator: scan leaves 286 and 289, glossary (printed pages unverified)

short.note: Bose's glossary: 'Kumbha — Water-pot; similar moulding used in pabhaga'. Behera's glossary: 'water pot; pitcher-shaped moulding of the pabhaga'.

short.text: The pata is a moulding with a square edge. It is used in the foot of the wall and in other bands of mouldings.

sources.locator: scan leaves 163, 173 and 291, glossary (printed pages unverified)

short.note: N.K. Bose's glossary (1932): 'Pata — Moulding with a square edge.'

short.text: The kani is a moulding shaped like a letter V lying on its side. It is one of the mouldings in the foot of the wall.

sources.locator: scan leaves 163 and 288, glossary (printed pages unverified)

short.note: N.K. Bose's glossary (1932): 'Moulding of the shape of a V placed sideways'. The scan reads the headword as 'Kant'; its place between Kalasa and Kanika and the index entry 'kani p.' show it is kani.

short.text: The jangha is the tall, upright face of the wall, above the foot mouldings.

long.text: Jangha is a body word for part of the leg. It has been translated both as 'shin' and as 'thigh'.
long.note: N.K. Bose (1932) translates jangha as 'shin'. Debala Mitra (ASI) and K.S. Behera translate it as 'thigh'. They agree on which part of the wall it is.

short.text: The bandhana is a band of mouldings that divides the jangha into a lower and an upper part. Its name means 'that which binds'.

sources.locator: scan leaves 143 and 285, glossary (printed pages unverified)

short.note: N.K. Bose's glossary (1932): 'That which binds; set of mouldings between janghas'; in his text, 'the bandhana or the bond'.

short.text: The tala jangha is the lower jangha, between the pabhaga and the bandhana.
The upara jangha is the upper jangha, between the bandhana and the baranda.
short.note: Spellings: upara jangha (Mitra), upar jangha (Bose).

short.text: The baranda is the set of mouldings that crowns the top of the wall, just below the tower or roof.
short.note: Also spelled varanda (Mitra, Behera).

short.text: A trianga bada is a wall in three parts: the foot (pabhaga), the tall middle (jangha) and the top band (baranda).
short.note: N.K. Bose (1932): the early temples 'have a bara composed of three elements, viz. pabhaga, jangha and baranda'.

long.text: Trianga means 'three-part'. It is a modern name, not an old builders' word.
long.note: N.K. Bose (1932): 'The tri-anga (a name coined to denote a three-segmented) bara'.

long.text: Early temples mostly have the three-part wall. The five-part wall is found in later temples.
long.note: N.K. Bose (1932) found that the Bhubaneswar temples he could date early 'have a bara composed of three elements', and that five parts appear 'only in the later temples'. Debala Mitra's ASI guide, describing Konark, says the wall has five divisions 'as in all Orissa temples'; that describes the fully developed temples. The dating rests on style.

short.text: A panchanga bada is a wall in five parts: pabhaga, tala jangha, bandhana, upara jangha and baranda.
short.note: Bose writes 'pancha-anga'.

short.text: The beki is the narrow round neck just above the tower. The word means 'neck' or 'throat'.
short.note: N.K. Bose calls it 'the throat'; Debala Mitra 'neck'. Behera: it 'separates the square gandi from the circular crowning elements'.

short.text: The amla (also called amalaka) is a big, flattened, ribbed round part near the top of the tower. It looks like a giant amla fruit.

sources.locator: scan leaves 107 and 284, glossary (printed pages unverified)

short.note: Mitra: 'fluted oblate spheroid resembling an amalaka fruit'. Bose: 'a flattened spheroid, ribbed at the sides and resembling an enormous fruit of the amalaki'.

short.text: The khapuri is a flattish, bell-shaped cap above the amla. Its name means 'skull'.
The kalasa is a part shaped like a water-pot, set on top of the khapuri.
short.note: K.S. Behera says the kalasa 'was sometimes made of gold'; Mitra records a copper kalasa at Konark.

short.text: The ayudha is the weapon or emblem of the temple's god, set at the top of the crown.
short.note: Bose: 'the ayudha or weapon of the deity to whom the temple is consecrated'. Mitra: 'sacred weapon or emblem'.

long.text: The emblem on top shows which god the temple is for. A Vishnu temple has a wheel (chakra); a Shiva temple has a trident or a linga.
long.note: K.S. Behera: 'A Visnu temple is crowned by a chakra, a Siva temple either a Trisula or a Linga. The Sun temple has a lotus finial.'

short.text: A flag, the dhvaja, is raised at the very top of the temple.
short.note: K.S. Behera: 'The dhvaja or banner is placed at the pinnacle of the temple.'

short.text: On a pidha roof, the crown has a big bell-shaped part called the ghanta, also called sri.

sources.locator: scan leaves 100 and 101, glossary (printed pages unverified)
scan leaves 108 and 287, glossary (printed pages unverified)

short.note: Bose: 'an enormous ribbed structure shaped like a bell'. Mitra: 'bell-shaped member in the finial of a pidha temple; it is also called sri'.

short.text: On a rekha tower, the corner strips are divided into storeys called bhumis. A small amla, the bhumi-amla, marks the top of each storey.

sources.locator: scan leaves 52 and 167, glossary (printed pages unverified)

short.note: Bose calls the bhumis 'planes', Behera 'levels'. Bose: each is 'surmounted by a miniature amla, called the bhumi-amla'.

short.text: A pidha is one flat, jutting layer of a pidha roof. The word means a flat wooden seat.
The pidhas are often grouped into tiers. Each tier is called a potala.
short.note: K.S. Behera: the gap between two potalas 'is known as kanti'.

short.text: A paga (also called a ratha) is an upright strip of the outer wall that steps forward. Inside, the walls are usually kept plain.

sources.locator: scan leaves 25 and 101, glossary (printed pages unverified)

short.note: Mitra: projections 'known in Orissan Silpa-sastras or architectural canons as rathas or pagas'. Bose: the inner walls 'are kept rigorously plain', though Mitra notes mouldings on the inner walls of Konark's porch.

short.text: The raha is the middle paga on each side of the temple. It sticks out the furthest.

sources.locator: scan leaves 26 and 101, glossary (printed pages unverified)

short.note: Bose records a second name for it: go-ratha or madhya-ratha. Behera: the side-shrine gods (parsvadevatas) sit in its niche.

short.text: The kanika is the corner paga, the outermost strip at each corner of the temple.
short.note: Also called kanika-paga (Mitra, Behera) or kanyasa (Bose).

short.text: On a five-strip (pancharatha) wall, the anuratha is the strip between the middle raha and the corner kanika.

sources.locator: scan leaves 26 and 100, glossary (printed pages unverified)

short.note: Mitra: 'projection next to the kanika-paga in pancha-ratha, sapta-ratha and nava-ratha temples'. On seven- and nine-strip walls the strip next to the raha is the anuraha, and the anuratha stays next to the kanika.

short.text: On seven- and nine-strip walls, an extra strip called the anuraha sits right next to the middle raha.
short.note: Mitra: 'projection next to the raha (central projection) in sapta-ratha and nava-ratha temples'.

short.text: A triratha temple has three pagas on each side: a raha in the middle and a kanika at each corner.
A pancharatha temple has five pagas on each side. The middle strip is stepped forward a second time.
A saptaratha temple has seven pagas on each side.
A navaratha temple has nine pagas on each side.
A torana is a gateway with an arch that stands on its own. The Mukteshvara Temple in Bhubaneswar has one in front: a round arch on two pillars.

sources.locator: scan leaves 214 and 388, glossary (printed pages unverified)

short.note: Percy Brown: 'This detached portal consists of two pillars supporting a round arch within a semi-circular shaped pediment'. K.C. Panigrahi: no torana is found at any other existing temple in Bhubaneswar; the remains of an earlier one were dug up at Dola-mandapa.
